title: Model Routing as a Cost-Reduction Primitive

questions.question: What is the core idea of model cascading?
options: Run two models in parallel and average the outputs
Run every request on the most expensive model first
Run a cheap model first, escalate to a frontier model only on low confidence or refusal
questions.explanation: The lesson defines model cascading as sending a request to a cheap model first and escalating to a frontier model only when confidence is low or the cheap model refuses -- the opposite of always using the most expensive model.

questions.question: Which four signals does the lesson list for routing decisions?
options: Task classification, prompt length, embedding similarity to known-hard set, and self-confidence from a first-pass
GPU temperature, fan speed, room humidity, time of day
questions.explanation: The lesson enumerates exactly these four routing signals: task classification, prompt length, embedding similarity to a known-hard bucket, and self-confidence (log-probs, refusals, hedging) from a first cheap-model pass.

questions.question: What is the expected latency profile of a cascade router?
options: About 1.2x median latency (cheap run plus verify), about 2x on escalated requests (~10% of traffic)
questions.explanation: The lesson states cascade routing costs about 1.2x median latency (the cheap run plus a confidence check) and about 2x on the roughly 10% of traffic that escalates to the frontier model.

questions.question: Which routing pattern adds 5-10ms latency up front and is fastest overall?
questions.explanation: The lesson lists pre-route (a classifier deciding the route before any model call) as adding only ~5-10ms of latency up front, making it the fastest overall pattern versus cascade or ensemble routing.

questions.question: What is cheap-model drift in routing?
options: The cheap model becomes more expensive
Cascade falls through to frontier 100% of the time
Task distribution shifts but the trained router keeps sending requests to the cheap model, silently degrading quality
A latency drift in the cheap model
questions.explanation: The lesson's drift scenario: the task distribution shifts over months (users ask harder questions) but the router's classifier, trained on old data, keeps sending the same share to the cheap model, so quality drops silently until someone notices.

questions.question: Which guard does the lesson recommend to catch routing drift?
options: Online quality metrics — thumbs-up/down per route, LLM-judge on held-out samples, escalation rate, refusal rate
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends gating routes with online quality metrics rather than only offline eval sets: per-route thumbs-up/down, an automated LLM-judge on a held-out sample, escalation rate, and refusal rate per route.
